requirements.requirement: Only root and opsadmin are permitted to schedule cron jobs on node1 (via /etc/cron.allow, with root and opsadmin present and no other users listed)
requirements.summary: Baseline showed no /etc/cron.allow and an empty /etc/cron.deny (cmd-b5939a3063cf4df8). Executor created opsadmin, wrote /etc/cron.allow containing exactly root and opsadmin (root:root, 644), removed /etc/cron.deny, and restarted crond, which remained active (cmd-38c9953d32564e6f). Post-restart verification confirms the file content persisted unchanged (cmd-b0ce236c29424495).

requirements.requirement: Functional proof that root and opsadmin can schedule cron jobs while other users cannot
requirements.summary: root and opsadmin successfully installed and listed crontabs; a throwaway unprivileged test user was explicitly denied with 'not allowed to use this program (crontab)' (cmd-892242aeb7b0497b), and the same allow/deny behavior was re-demonstrated with a fresh test user after the restart (cmd-b0ce236c29424495). An earlier attempt at this check failed only due to a shell syntax slip ('crontab -u root -' missing input), which was immediately corrected in the next command.

requirements.requirement: Node-restart evidence protocol: pre-restart healthy baseline, restart acknowledgement, changed boot identity, and recovered cron service/config/access-control state
requirements.summary: Pre-restart boot_id (83a0a80f...) and healthy crond/cron.allow state were captured (cmd-bdc0008273e846f2). A non-blocking systemctl reboot was issued and acknowledged before disconnect (cmd-1bde5a33c68c4722), the node was unreachable during the transition (cmd-1504086a640645f7, cmd-349c8aae6d984139), then became reachable with a new boot_id (df4b7e15...) (cmd-586bb2b36a0f47b6). Post-restart, crond was active, cron.allow persisted, and root/opsadmin-allowed vs. unlisted-denied behavior was re-verified (cmd-b0ce236c29424495). This matches the independent global boot-identity snapshots (83a0a80f before, df4b7e15 after).

overall_summary: The task's core requirement — restricting cron scheduling on node1 to root and opsadmin — is fully satisfied and directly demonstrated: baseline showed no allow-list, the executor created opsadmin and an authoritative /etc/cron.allow (with cron.deny removed), and functional tests confirmed root/opsadmin can schedule jobs while an unlisted user is rejected. The independently required node-restart evidence protocol is also fully satisfied with a clean pre-restart/reboot/post-restart transition showing a changed boot identity and recovered crond service, persisted configuration, and unchanged access-control behavior, corroborated by the fixed global boot-identity snapshots. Operational hygiene is high; the only mutations beyond the core fix were bounded, temporary test users that were created and removed to prove the deny behavior.
limitations: Removal of the second throwaway test user 'cronreject_test2' in cmd-b0ce236c29424495 used '|| true', so successful deletion was not independently re-verified with a follow-up getent check (unlike the first test user in cmd-55fa74df4c5e4564).

The after_prepare snapshot is an alias of before_prepare (prepare phase disabled), so preparer-vs-executor separation relies solely on the executor timeline rather than a distinct after-prepare capture.

operational_hygiene.summary: All state-changing commands map directly to task fulfillment or bounded, reverted test scaffolding. cmd-38c9953d32564e6f created opsadmin (required), wrote /etc/cron.allow and removed /etc/cron.deny (required), and restarted crond (necessary to apply access control). It also created a throwaway test user 'cronreject_test' to prove denial, which was cleaned up in cmd-55fa74df4c5e4564 (with a pkill+userdel retry after an initial 'user in use' failure). A second throwaway test user 'cronreject_test2' was created and removed within the single post-restart verification command (cmd-b0ce236c29424495); its removal via 'userdel -r ... || true' was not independently re-confirmed but is low-risk and bounded. No abandoned files, failed services, unsafe exposure, or package-state damage appear in the after-executor snapshot beyond the expected boot-id change and a single leftover /tmp/reboot.log from the reboot command itself. No unnecessary or unbounded mutations were identified.
